- **refined** (ch-008.txt): Notes-section weaknesses in Moyo's sourcing (a fair-presentation caveat): (1) her own endnote 9 to ch.2 says democracy and growth studies are 'cautious... no direct link per se', which softens the main-text claim that growth must precede democracy; (2) the Mobutu $5bn figure is sourced to a cached web search for a Transparency International PDF, not a primary study; (3) the Uganda 20-cents-per-dollar figure comes from World Bank expenditure tracking surveys of 1991-95 and is not a 2008 figure; (4) the Burnside-Dollar rebuttal rests on Easterly, Levine and Roodman (2003) 'New Data, New Doubts' (a genuine replication); (5) the 'poverty 11 to 66 per cent' claim has no endnote at all in the notes (check: no entry for it under ch.3), so the source is untraceable from the book; (6) bibliography cites Radelet, Collier, Easterly, Sachs-style critics, Rodrik, Landes, Ferguson. Meredith's The State of Africa is cited for privatisation (note 7). Use for the notes file 'limits'
- **refined** (ch-009.txt): CURRENT-DATA CHECK (web, 01/11/2026) of Moyo's dated numbers: (1) Aid: OECD preliminary 2024 DAC net ODA $212.1bn (0.33 per cent of GNI), first fall in five years; net bilateral ODA to Africa $42bn, to sub-Saharan Africa $36bn (preliminary); final OECD 2024 statistics on a broader measure show ODA to sub-Saharan Africa $66.5bn; so the aid-to-Africa figure depends on measure (bilateral vs total incl. multilateral). Her '~$37bn in 2006' and '13-15 per cent of GDP' are not comparable without matching measure. (2) Poverty: Our World in Data/World Bank PIP puts sub-Saharan Africa extreme poverty ($3.00/day line, 2021 PPP) at roughly 43 per cent now, and the region holds the large majority (~70 per cent per a secondary summary of the 2024 report) of the world's extreme poor; her 1998 '66 per cent' ($1/day, old method) is not comparable with the current line. Verify against PIP before use. (3) Remittances to SSA ~$54bn in 2023 (World Bank, 06/2024; Nigeria $19.5bn, Ghana $4.6bn, Kenya $4.2bn), average cost 7.9 per cent of $200 in 2023Q4, against her 2006 $20bn and ~20 per cent fee. Sources: OECD press release 04/2025; World Bank Migration and Development Brief 06/2024; OWID/PIP
- **contradicted** (ch-002.txt): Moyo errors/loose claims to NOT repeat: (1) she calls Harry Dexter White 'US Secretary of State' (he was a US Treasury official; Marshall was Secretary of State); (2) she says the Soviet Union 'financed' Lumumba and Mengistu as 'Africa's greatest communists' (Lumumba was a nationalist, not a declared communist; Soviet help came only after Western refusal; Mengistu was a Marxist-Leninist military ruler) so keep course wording; (3) Kariba 'completed 1977' describes the later north-bank power station: the dam wall was completed 1959 [check]. Verify before citing
- **contradicted** (ch-005.txt): Internal inconsistency in Moyo's China numbers (checked by arithmetic on her own text): she gives China's investment in Africa as $900m in 2004 (out of $15bn received, up from $20m in 1975) but also 'Chinese FDI to Africa totalled $30bn between 2000 and 2005' and 'stock $100bn by mid-2007'; a $900m annual flow cannot sum to $30bn over five years, and official Chinese FDI-stock figures for Africa in this period were far lower than $100bn (the larger numbers mix in loans, contracts and pledges). Treat all three as unreliable; for current figures use the China Africa Research Initiative (SAIS-CARI) loan and FDI data or MOFCOM [check current]. The Tanzam (Tazara) railway, 1,860 km, built 1970s for about $500m, is correct as a Chinese-aid example and is a good Module 4/6 cross-reference; FOCAC Beijing summit 11/2006 (40+ leaders) also checks out
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Moyo's headline claims (2009, Dead Aid), via Ferguson's foreword and her introduction: over US$1 trillion in development aid to Africa in 50 years (foreword says over $300bn since 1970); the most aid-dependent countries averaged -0.2 per cent growth over thirty years; African poverty rate 'rose from 11 per cent to 66 per cent 1970-1998' at peak aid; Mobutu stole about $5bn, equal to Zaire's external debt; $10bn a year leaves Africa; China invested $900m in Africa in 2004 vs $20m in 1975. Her thesis: aid is a curse like natural resources (corruption, conflict, kills enterprise); radical proposal: aid taps shut off in five years; replace with bonds, Chinese FDI, trade, microfinance/remittances. Ferguson himself says 'the correlation is suggestive, even if the causation may be debated'. All figures are 2009-era and the 11-to-66 per cent poverty figure and the aid-causes-poverty claim are contested: label [CONTESTED] and [check current]; verify the poverty trend against current World Bank (PovcalNet/PIP) and the $1 trillion figure against OECD DAC
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Moyo's rosier 2008 'state of Africa' list: growth around 5 per cent, over half of 48 sub-Saharan countries holding regular free elections, 16 stock markets with 2008 market cap about $200bn (excluding South Africa); drivers = commodity prices, market policies of the late 1980s (structural adjustment dividend), improved politics. Useful counterpoint in Module 6 structural adjustment: she credits the late-1980s market reforms for the 2000s recovery, which is a minority-to-contested reading (Rodney/others would dispute). Dated: 2008 commodity boom ended 2014-16 [check current]
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Moyo's 'state of Africa' dated statistics (2007-08 sources, all [check current]): over half of ~700m Africans on under $1 a day (the old $1 line, since replaced by the World Bank's $2.15 then $3.00/day international poverty line); sub-Saharan poverty count nearly doubled 1981-2002 (true in headcount because population grew fast, while the share began falling after the mid-1990s per later World Bank work); life expectancy ~50 (now much higher, around 60+), 1 in 7 children dead before five (now about 1 in 14), Polity IV list of 11 autocracies, Bongo 40 years in power; eleven civil wars since 1996. Use as snapshot of the 2008 aid-critique, not as current data
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Moyo's aid history timeline (useful for Module 6 background): Bretton Woods 07/1944 (44 countries); Marshall Plan 1948-52 about $13bn to 14 countries; aid to Africa ~$100m by 1960, $950m by 1965, ~$36bn cumulative by end of 1970s; oil shocks 1973 and 1979; floating-rate loans, Volcker-era rates rise -> debt crisis: Mexico default 12/08/1982, eleven African defaults (Angola, Cameroon, Congo, Ivory Coast, Gabon, Gambia, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Tanzania, Zambia); Africa's debt service $2bn (1975) to $8bn (1982); IMF Structural Adjustment Facility created. Her point: 1970s loans (not grants) fuelled the debt that preceded structural adjustment. Consistent with mainstream accounts; the claim that aid itself caused the crisis is hers
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Structural adjustment as Moyo tells it (matches Module 6 structure but with a different verdict): 1980s IMF/World Bank programmes (SAF/ESAF) paired budget support with privatisation, trade liberalisation, civil service cuts (six countries cut 10 per cent+ of civil service 1986-96; state share of corporate equity from almost 90 to 10 per cent in six years; Zambia Airways closed); 1989 Washington Consensus; net reverse flow of about $15bn a year from poor to rich countries 1987-89; emerging-market debt over $1tn by end 1980s; oil fell $38 (1980) to $15 (1986). She treats this as a continuation of the aid model, not as a free-market cure. Counter-positions (Rodney: structural dependence; mainstream critics: SAPs cut health and education) to sit beside
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Moyo on Cold War aid and governance eras: dictators propped up (Amin, Mobutu, Mengistu, Doe), Bokassa's 1977 coronation $22m, Nigeria ranked most corrupt of 54 countries in 1996 (Transparency International CPI 0.69/10, a dated ranking); 1990s turn to governance and democracy ('any improvements achieved in spite of (nominal) democracy', a contested claim); aid falls in 1990s (net ODA $17bn to $12bn by 1999 per Moyo; ODA/GNI 0.38 per cent 1982 to 0.22 per cent 1997); 2000s 'glamour aid': Live Aid 13/07/1985, Jubilee Debt Campaign, Bono/Geldof, Gleneagles 2005. Quotes Kagame: '$300 billion since 1970 with little to show'. Moyo's own 'more than $2 trillion over fifty years' is a world-wide figure; the earlier '$1 trillion to Africa' figure is hers; check against OECD DAC series [check current]
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Moyo's six counter-arguments to 'aid works' (useful structure for a Module 6 debate card): (1) Marshall Plan: peaked at 2.5 per cent of recipient GDP, never over 3 per cent, finite, reconstruction not development; Africa now receives ~15 per cent of GDP in aid (dated 2008, check current); (2) IDA graduates (22 countries, only Botswana, Equatorial Guinea, Swaziland from Africa); Botswana aid was ~20 per cent of national income in 1960s, 1.6 per cent by 2000, average real per capita growth 6.8 per cent 1968-2001; (3) conditionalities failed (a World Bank study 'as much as 85 per cent' of aid diverted [check source]; Svensson: no link between reform and aid disbursement); (4) good-policy environments: Burnside-Dollar 2000 later failed replication (she says 'tenuous, not robust'; this is a fair summary of the later literature, e.g. Easterly et al.); (5) democracy: she argues autocracy can be better for early growth (Pinochet, East Asia), calls for 'benevolent dictator' - highly contested (Acemoglu/Robinson, Sen and others; evidence mixed); 'aid-funded democracy' claim. Present her policy conclusions as one position and put Sen/Acemoglu or the mainstream evidence beside it
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Moyo's strongest claim and its weakest numbers: (a) 'between 1970 and 1998, poverty in Africa rose from 11 per cent to 66 per cent' (~600 million of 1 billion) [CONTESTED, check current]: widely criticised because it is a per-head $1/day estimate drawn from a single study using a method that later work (Sala-i-Martin & Pinkovskiy; World Bank PIP) revised, and because the same series shows African extreme poverty falling slowly after the mid-1990s; do not use as a measured fact. (b) Easterly's Zambia counterfactual (aid converted to growth would give ~$20,000 per head by early 1990s vs under $500) is a thought experiment, not a finding. (c) 'Most aid-dependent countries grew -0.2 per cent for 30 years' is her citation, correlation not causation (aid goes to poor, conflict-affected countries). (d) The 'mosquito-net maker' parable is an illustration with no data; later evidence on free nets is mixed. The counter-view (Sachs, 'big push'; Burnside-Dollar debate) should stand beside
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Moyo on corruption and aid: Mobutu $5bn (TI) and Abacha $5bn with $700m later returned; IMF's Blumenthal memo 1978 on Zaire ('no repeat no prospect' of repayment) followed by IMF's largest African loan and $700m more over ten years; Chiluba embezzlement (Mwanawasa alleges up to $80m) while Zambia received $1.5bn from the World Bank; World Bank 1992 OED: tranches released near 100 per cent even when conditionality compliance under 50 per cent; 1997 study: 72 per cent of adjustment lending 1980-96 to poor compliers; claims 'World Bank complicit in roughly $100bn corrupted' from a 2004 US Senate hearing (a witness claim, [CONTESTED]); Uganda: only 20 cents of each $1 of education spending reached schools in the 1990s (Reinikka-Svensson survey, later reformed, [dated]). Use as evidence of the 'Cold War client' story for Module 4/6 (links to Hochschild's Mobutu chapter)
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Moyo's mechanism chain (core of her thesis): aid -> weaker tax link and accountability, rent-seeking, crowding out of savings/private investment, inflation, Dutch disease (aid inflow strengthens currency, hurts exports), absorption bottlenecks and sterilisation costs (Uganda 2005: $700m aid-related bonds costing $110m/yr interest), conflict over control of aid (cites Grossman, Maren on Somalia food aid, RUF diamond deal), 'aid is ~13 per cent of GDP and 10 per cent of public spending' (2008 averages, dated). Also claims '40 million Africans died in civil wars in five decades' (source not given here, [CONTESTED]). The micro-macro paradox and Dutch disease are real mainstream concepts; her assertion that these effects dominate is the contested step (IMF Rajan-Subramanian findings exist but are mixed). Intellectual lineage: Peter Bauer (aid taxes poor in the West to enrich elites in the South), Easterly, Collier; Moyo says none gave an alternative menu. Fictional 'Republic of Dongo' is an illustrative composite, not data
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Moyo's alternative finance, step 1 (bonds): Ghana $750m ten-year Eurobond 09/2007, Gabon $1bn 10/2007; S&P says 35 African economies had bond access in the 1970s-80s; argues returns on emerging-market debt (12 per cent in 2006; 35 per cent in 2007) and low correlation make African bonds attractive; wants aid cut over five to ten years, not instantly (Botswana is her model; she allows modest aid). Dated and since tested: Zambia defaulted on its Eurobonds in 11/2020 and Ghana in 12/2022 (and Ethiopia in 2023), after the 2010s borrowing wave; so her 2009 optimism about market borrowing is a clear case to label [dated]; debt sustainability and China lending are the live debate [check current IMF/World Bank DSA]. Also her claim emerging-market debt is 'countercyclical' is overtaken by the 2008 crisis and 2020 shocks
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Moyo's definition of her own proposal (use when presenting her fairly): not an overnight stop; 'gradual but uncompromising' reduction of systematic aid over five to ten years; room for modest, well-designed aid (Botswana as poster child); emergency and charity aid excluded from her target. Foreword (Ferguson) frames it as 'five years then shut off'; the book's own text is milder. Course should quote the book's version, not the foreword's
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Bond-market chapter dated claims (all 2006-08): only three African countries (South Africa, Ghana, Gabon) issued international bonds in the prior decade; 15 African countries rated since 2003; Africa's share of emerging-market bond debt ~$10m (sic, likely a typo for far more); World Bank concessional loans cost ~0.75 per cent vs ~10 per cent for emerging-market bonds in 2007; EM spreads fell from 30 to 5 per cent 1996-2006; she argues defaults are forgiven by markets and calls for local-currency bonds (EIB 125bn kwacha note 11/02/2008; GEMLOC launched 10/2007). By the late 2010s about two dozen African states had issued Eurobonds and by 2020-23 Zambia, Ghana and Ethiopia had defaulted: [dated, check current]. Her 'markets are forgiving' line is exactly what the later debt-restructuring debates (G20 Common Framework) dispute
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Moyo on FDI: sub-Saharan Africa got $17bn FDI in 2006 vs $37bn aid; under 1 per cent of global flows (down from ~5 per cent a decade earlier); World Bank Doing Business time/procedure figures for company start-up (Cameroon 426 days in her text) are dated and the Doing Business index was discontinued by the World Bank in 09/2021 after data-irregularity reviews: label [dated; do not use]; Uganda poverty fall 56 to 32 per cent 1998-2002 (dollar-a-day, older method); she argues Africa does not attract FDI due to bureaucracy and corruption, with Zambia mining royalties cut to 0.6 per cent in the late 1990s then raised to 3 per cent; cross-check Zambia's mining-tax history and 'Chambishi' sales. This is the 'privatisation and low royalties' episode (Module 6) with a positive spin; note counter-view that low royalties cost Zambia revenue
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): China-in-Africa details (2004-06, dated): CNOOC ~$3bn for 45 per cent of a Nigerian oilfield (01/2006); 900-mile pipeline and $20bn+ invested in Sudan; Angola overtook Saudi Arabia as China's top oil supplier in H1 2006 (~20 per cent of China's oil imports; Africa ~30 per cent); Congo-Brazzaville sells almost half its crude to China; Sudan 64 per cent of oil exports to China in 2006; Benguela railway rehabilitation; $8.3bn Lagos-Kano rail deal. Her framing 'the Chinese are our friends' (benefits: no governance conditionality, infrastructure) is one side; the other side (debt, labour practices, resource-for-loans, Sudan's war, Zambia/Angola/Kenya debt, Dar-Zambia Tazara needs) is not in her text, so the course's Module 7 Sudan/AU and Module 6 debt materials should add a counter-position [check current]
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Trade chapter claims (all 2003-08 data): OECD farm subsidies ~$300bn in 2005 (nearly 3x OECD aid); 'Africa loses $500bn a year' from trade restrictions (a very large, weakly sourced number: label [CONTESTED]); US cotton subsidies $4bn in 2003 (Oxfam: more than Burkina Faso's GDP), West African cotton complaint to WTO 05/2003 by Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali; EU sugar tariffs over 300 per cent; intra-African trade only ~10 per cent of exports and African average tariffs 34 per cent on other African agricultural goods; Africa's share of world trade ~1 per cent from 3 per cent sixty years earlier; AGOA 2000 and EU Everything But Arms 2001 named; China pledge of $100bn annual trade by 2010. Intra-African trade and the AfCFTA (launched 2018-21) are the current counterparts [check current]. The farm-subsidy argument is shared by many aid-sceptics and aid-supporters alike (Oxfam), so it is one of her stronger points
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): AGOA/EBA reality check from Moyo (2003-2008 data): AGOA exports >$14bn in 2003 but ~80 per cent petroleum and 90 per cent of benefits to Nigeria, South Africa, Gabon, Lesotho; EBA preference covered just 0.02 per cent of LDC exports to EU in 2001; Africa's trade partners 2008: EU 26 per cent (down from 40 per cent in 1996), US 18, China 11; Africa-China trade $45bn in 2007 (about 2 per cent of China's trade); 90 per cent of African exports to China from five countries (Angola, Sudan, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Mauritania); intra-African barriers over 30 per cent; trade-share of GDP examples. These are the 2008 baseline; by the 2020s China-Africa trade exceeded $250bn a year (2022: ~$282bn, official Chinese customs figure) [check current]
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Microfinance as 'banking on the unbankable' (ch.9 opening): Grameen Bank (Yunus, Nobel Peace Prize 2006): 97 per cent women borrowers, default under 2 per cent, 'No Donor Money, No Loans' since 1995, 8-12 per cent interest; Zambia: ~500,000 of 10m formally employed, micro-lender default under 5 per cent (2008 claim). Later evidence is more cautious: randomised evaluations (Banerjee, Duflo et al., 2015, in six countries) found modest average effects and no transformation of poverty; 2010 Andhra Pradesh over-indebtedness crisis; Grameen's later governance troubles [check current]. Present her view as optimistic baseline, add the RCT caution
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Remittances and savings (dated claims): remittances to Africa ~$20bn in 2006 (vs Latin America $68bn, Asia $113bn); sending costs: $80 of $100 arrives (about 20 per cent fee); Nigeria $5bn, South Africa $1.5bn, Angola $1bn; Somalia ~40 per cent of GDP; World Bank 2008 'Beyond Aid' estimates diaspora bonds $5-10bn and securitised remittances $17bn; M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007 (she says April 2007; widely given as March 2007 [check]). Hernando de Soto's 'dead capital' claim (poor hold assets 40x all aid since 1945) is his, not measured data, and land-titling programmes have had mixed evidence. Current remittance data (World Bank/KNOMAD) and M-Pesa's scale should replace these [check current]; remittances now exceed aid and FDI to many African states
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Moyo's conclusion and policy asks (for fair presentation): aid shut off over five years with emergency relief exempt; replace with the five channels; strengthen institutions (Landes list); she endorses conditional cash transfers (Brazil, Mexico, Nicaragua, Peru) and direct per-head transfers as better than government-to-government aid; claims without aid Mugabe 'might have been long gone' (Zimbabwe got $300m in 2006: contested, Western aid to Zimbabwe was largely humanitarian under sanctions); warns 'the Chinese are coming... when they own the banks, the land and the resources their crusade will be over' and says Singapore shows peace can prevail without democracy (opinion). Justin Lin Yifu became World Bank chief economist 2008 (correct). Includes terrorism-haven and migration arguments for Western self-interest
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Moyo's treatment of 'other explanations' (geography via Diamond, colonial borders, ethnic fractionalisation via Collier, institutions via Landes/Ferguson/Rodrik): she accepts they matter in part but says none 'should condemn Africa'; she argues ethnic diversity explanation is a dead end (born a Zulu, always a Zulu is false). Collier's civil war costs ~4x annual GDP and neighbour spill-over ~half of GDP; Nigeria 'almost 400 tribes', ~1,000 tribes in sub-Saharan Africa (ethnic counts vary widely by method; label [ESTIMATE])
- **note** (ch-006.txt): Moyo answers China critics: Pew 06/2007 (10 African countries; favourable views of China at least 2:1 in almost every country, e.g. Ivory Coast and Mali over 90 per cent), Sudan/Darfur ('more than 200,000 killed', a 2008-era estimate, UN said 300,000 and Sudan govt ~10,000; contested [ESTIMATE]), EIB's Maystadt on Chinese lenders undercutting social standards, Nigerian rail $9bn Chinese offer vs a $5m World Bank project. She argues Africans can regulate Chinese firms themselves. Dated opinion data (2007): check Afrobarometer/Pew for current attitudes [check current]; many later studies find mixed views and growing debt concern
- **note** (ch-007.txt): Arithmetic check on the mosquito-net parable: ch.3 says ten workers supporting 'upwards of fifteen relatives each' = 150 dependants; ch.9 says '176 people (one owner, ten workers and their 165 dependants)'. 1+10+165 = 176 is consistent internally, but 165 is not 150; the second figure silently adds 15 dependants for the owner. Trivial, but an example of the illustrative (not empirical) status of her anecdotes. Also Dongo's 'current mix' sums: aid 75 + capital markets 3 + trade 5 + FDI 5 = 88, leaving 12 for remittances/savings; her target mix 5+30+30+10+25 = 100 (checked)
- **note** (ch-007.txt): Arithmetic check on the 'five-year phone call' plan: Dongo's aid share falls '14 per cent every year' from 75 to 5 per cent: 75-14=61, -28=47, -42=33, -56=19, -70=5, so it is 14 percentage points a year (not 14 per cent), and reaches exactly 5 after five years; checked and consistent. Note Kagame's quoted aid total is $300bn since 1970 in ch.2 but '$400bn in 50 years' in ch.10 (the Time interview, 09/2007): her own text uses different totals (00bn / $400bn / $1tn / $2tn) for different windows and recipients, so never quote a single 'aid to Africa' number from the book without the window

### 1

- **contradicted** (ch-002.txt): Moyo repeats the popular line that the 1885 Berlin Conference carried out 'the ill-conceived partitioning of Africa' and drew arbitrary borders (14 nations attended). Hochschild (ch.9) explicitly calls this a myth: Berlin set ground rules (free trade in the Congo basin, navigation, effective occupation) and settled the Congo mouth; the actual borders came from many later bilateral treaties and conquests. Keep the course wording precise: Berlin = ground rules and recognition of the Congo claim; borders = bilateral treaties 1885-1914. Moyo is a popular-economics source here, not a historian
